title: Application of Johnson–Mehl–Avrami-Kolmogorov theory in modelling porosity evolution and resistivity in metallic powder compaction
abstract: Abstract In the current study, the mathematical analogy between the Johnson–Mehl–Avrami-Kolmogorov equation and the equations describing density, the effective cross-sectional area and porosity evolution in compaction of metallic powders is presented. In addition, the density evolution in the early stages due to particle arrangement and elastic deformation are considered. The study provides an insight to the average (mean field) evolution of the regions occupied by the particles by demonstrating the mathematical analogy to growth and impingement of phase regions in solid state phase transformations. In a sense, the growth and impingement of the cross-sectional areas of particles can be interpreted as one phase (the solid particle) growing into another phase (the pore region). In addition to presenting the analogy and the interpretation, a slight geometrically based fine-tuning to the electrical resistivity equation is developed, which shows improvement in fitting when comparing to previously presented equation.
journal: Journal of Materials Science: Materials Theory

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: As described in (Montes et al.  16 ; Montes and Ternero  23 ), porosity is a key microstructural parameter that governs the mechanical, thermal, and electrical properties of powder-based materials. In powder metallurgy and sintering processes, understanding how porosity evolves during compaction is essential for predicting final material performance. Numerous studies have been constructed to model the effective properties of porous materials, particularly electrical conductivity, as a function of porosity (Clerk  5 ; Fricke  8 ; Murabayashi et al.  24 ; Loeb  13 ; Aivasov and Domashnev  1 ; Meyer  15 ; Schulz  34 ).

Early models, such as those by Maxwell ( 5 ), Fricke ( 8 ), and Loeb ( 13 ), provided foundational expressions for normalized electrical and thermal conductivity and porosity. Bal’shin ( 35 ) developed microscopic theory relating density, porosity, contact cross section and electrical conductivity. More recent formulations, including those by McLachlan [ 14 ] and Montes et al. ( 17 ,  23 ), have applied critical porosity thresholds and tap porosity parameters to better reflect the behavior of sintered powders.

Complementing this, Montes and Ternero ( 23 ) developed a finite difference model for Electrical Resistance Sintering (ERS), capturing the coupled electrical, thermal, and mechanical behavior of powder compacts. Their simulator, implemented in Excel with Visual Basic for Applications (VBA), models the time-dependent evolution of porosity and thermal energy release, incorporating temperature-dependent material properties and oxide breakdown phenomena. The model was validated against experimental data, showing good agreement in porosity and thermal energy evolution under varying current intensities and heating durations.

Alternative approaches have also explored microstructural influences on conductivity. Slesar et al. ( 38 ), Danninger et al. ( 6 ), and Simchi et al. ( 37 ) investigated the role of plain porosity and particle connectivity, linking electrical behavior to mechanical properties. These studies emphasize the importance of accurate porosity characterization, including tap density measurements (Montes and Ternero  23 ), and the limitations of models that rely solely on empirical fitting parameters.

In the present work, we establish a mathematical analogy between the equations describing porosity evolution during powder compaction (Montes et al.,  16 ; Montes, and Ternero  23 ) and the Johnson–Mehl–Avrami-Kolmogorov (JMAK) theory (Starink  39 ), which has been originally used in context of phase transformations (Porter and Easterling  30 ; Pohjonen et al.,  25 ,  26 ,  27 ,  28 ), but many contemporary studies have extended its use to new domains (Shirzad and Viney  36 ; Pohjonen et al.,  29 ). In the current study we show that the JMAK framework, originally developed to describe nucleation, growth, and impingement of transforming regions (Avrami  2 ,  3 ), provides a new interpretation of the densification process in terms of phase region evolution. From the observation that the inelastic strain can be connected to the extended volume fraction in JMAK theory, we derive a unified expression that links porosity, density, and effective surface area evolution during inelastic deformation. This mathematical analogy enables a geometrical interpretation of effective area region and density growth and the mathematical concept of overlap of the growing regions.

By integrating insights from porosity and conductivity modeling (Montes et al.,  16 ; Clerk  5 ; Fricke  8 ; Murabayashi et al.,  24 ; Loeb  13 ; Aivazov and Domashnev  1 ; Meyer  15 ; Schulz  34 ; McLachlan  14 ; Montes et al.,  17 ), ERS simulation (Montes and Ternero  23 ), and phase transformation theory (Starink  39 ; Avrami  2 ,  3 ; Christian  4 ), this study presents a new interpretation of the evolution of porosity and electrical resistivity in powder compaction processes.

sections.heading: JMAK theory
paragraphs: It is the main thesis of this article to mathematically demonstrate that the porosity evolution equations describing plastic deformation in (Montes and Ternero  23 ) are mathematically analogous to JMAK theory (Starink  39 ; Porter and Easterling  30 ; Avrami  2 ,  3 ) and it can be applied to describe average growth and impingement of particle regions during compaction of powders in plastic region. While the current analysis elucidates the mathematical sameness of the mean field evolution equation, the apparent physical mechanisms in phase evolution and pore/density evolution are distinct. Phase evolution occurs e.g. due to crystal structure change due atom re-arrangement at the phase interfaces due to thermodynamically favoured conditions. On the other hand, the porosity evolution in compression occurs due to inelastic deformation, which consists of particle plastic deformation and re-arrangement of particles. However, it is noted that both phase transitions and inelastic deformation can be considered as thermodynamic phenomena (Porter and Easterling  30 ; Rice  33 ), so in this broader context, they share the same fundamental basis.

sections.heading: Compression due to elastic deformation
paragraphs: Purely elastic stage in compression is likely to be very small in comparison to particle re-arrangement and plastic deformation, since in the early stages particles can quite easily move, and during compression there are likely to be small contact points between particles, where the stress will very rapidly exceed plastic limit during loading.

sections.heading: Compression due to inelastic deformation
paragraphs: The introduction of particles to a given plane due to their movement in the vertical direction (in the plane normal direction) during deformation can be interpreted to correspond to nucleation in the JMAK theory because geometrically they create new growing regions to the intersecting plane in a similar way as nucleation does in the context of phase transformations. This description could qualitatively link the geometrical effects of porosity and phase evolution, but in the current study, only the resultant effective inelastic deformation is considered, the growth of the particles and their movement in vertical direction are not explicitly described.

Electrical and thermal resistivities of compacted powders
paragraphs: Due to evolution of particle contacts in compression, the electrical and thermal conductivity of the porous aggregate changes.

Regarding the electrical resistivity in particular, a slight fine-tuning to the resistivity equation given in [Avrami  2 ] is now proposed to accommodate the condition where conductivity is essentially zero, based on the physical and geometrical condition where the particles are everywhere separated by a small amount from their initial position (the position they acquired when they were loaded to the compaction chamber) so they do not touch each other in the new position. In addition to providing better physical basis, this consideration also leads to a slightly better fit to the experimental data in comparison of the one shown in (Montes and Ternero  23 ).

sections.heading: Quantification of volume, area and contact percolation through JMAK theory
paragraphs: The Eqs. ( 29 ) and ( 30 ) provide a direct connection of the area and volume percolation to the JMAK equation, although in reality, a size distribution of particles can exist instead of constant radius.

sections.heading: Discussion and conclusions
paragraphs: As referred in the text, current analysis presents derivations from the previously published equations for metal powder compaction (Montes and Ternero  23 ), which yield the mathematical analogy between the extened and real transformed fractions of the JMAK theory. As a consequence, the derived equations are valid in the range where the original equations are valid. Therefore, if there are phenomena not included in the original equations, they are not described by the current derivation. Brittle powders behave differently, so at present the equations in this work cannot be expected to describe them. Whether the equations presented here might hold for such powders, would need to be experimentally studied.

In the current study, the following advances were described: Mathematical analogy between the JMAK equation and the evolution equation of porosity during metallic powder compaction (Montes et al.,  16 ; Montes and Ternero  23 ) was described as shown in Eq. ( 13 ) and Eqs. ( 16 ,  19 ,  20 ). The correspondence between the JMAK theory and porosity provides geometrical interpretation of the growth and impingement of the average area occupied by the particles in the planes with surface normal in the compaction direction. The overlap of the extended area/volume of the particles in JMAK theory provides understanding on the impingement and growth of particle surface areas depicted in Figs.  4  and  5 . Expressions relating the effective surface area and density evolution to the porosity and inelastic deformation were derived and presented in Eqs. ( 21 ,  22 ). These expressions provide new interpretations on the evolution of the different quantities in powder compaction. The fine-tuned geometrically and physically motivated improved Eq. ( 25 ) describing resistivity as function of porosity, incorporating the porosity value at which resistivity becomes infinite was presented. The method for fitting the equation parameters using linear fit, Eq. ( 26 ) was presented, and the fitting result was shown in Figs.  1  and  6 .

These points provide insights to the average geometrical evolution and its mathematical description by connecting JMAK theory to the porosity and resistivity equations, fine-tuning of the equations and new interpretations of the connections of the effective normal surface area, density and resistivity evolution during compaction. The application of the JMAK theory to describe the powder densification provides an interpretation that the regions occupied by the particles can be considered as one phase and the pores as another phase. The plastic deformation then results to the growth of the particle regions to the pore regions in mathematical analogy with phase transformations in solid state.

In future, it would be interesting to observe the growth mechanism of the particle filled regions towards the pores. This could be achieved with interrupted compression tests, and it could provide additional information on the rearrangement and growth kinetics.
